Retries need limits because they are load multipliers. When a dependency slows or fails, every client retrying increases traffic precisely when capacity is scarce, risking congestion collapse and thundering herds. Unbounded retries also consume threads, connections, memory, and quotas, starving healthy work and delaying definitive failure, which can make outages longer and harder to diagnose. They can duplicate non-idempotent side effects—payments, emails, writes—unless constrained and made safe. Limits enforce predictable latency and cost: max attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, per-request/per-client retry budgets, deadlines, and circuit breakers. These controls spread load, cap amplification, surface persistent faults, and preserve capacity for recovery. In short, retries are useful only when bounded; unlimited retries turn transient failures into systemic ones.
